narrative:
The model estimated a 51% chance that you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt. That is just over a coin flip, not a certainty, but it was enough for the application to be denied because the process treats a predicted failure as a risk signal. Your gender and race were not used in this prediction.

The denial was driven most strongly by your third-year class-rank decile. You are in the first decile, while accepted students average around the sixth decile. This was the top factor and it pushed the prediction toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA was the second most influential factor. At 3.20 it is essentially in line with the accepted average of 3.23, and it pushed slightly toward passing. Your family income bracket was third. Being in the middle-income group is common among accepted students—it is the second-largest group after upper-middle income—so it modestly pushed toward passing rather than explaining the rejection.

The decisive concern is therefore your third-year academic standing, not your GPA or family background. Next, ask admissions to explain how the prediction was used and whether you can provide context for your third-year rank. If possible, strengthen your academic record, seek advising about improving your class standing, and consider whether retaking the LSAT or submitting additional evidence of readiness would help a future application. Reapplication is more persuasive if you can show concrete improvement in the area that drove the denial.
